title: YOU MARRIED AS VIRGINS. SO WHY DOES YOUR MARRIAGE BED FEEL LIKE A PLACE OF FEAR INSTEAD OF LOVE?
paragraphs: YOU MARRIED AS VIRGINS. SO WHY DOES YOUR MARRIAGE BED FEEL LIKE A PLACE OF FEAR INSTEAD OF LOVE?

You waited. You prayed. You honored God with your bodies. But nobody prepared you for the tears, the silence, the painful expectations, and the shame that sometimes follow the wedding night. What if the problem isn't that you failed God—but that you were never taught the whole biblical truth about intimacy, tenderness, and grace?
The wedding was beautiful.

She wore white. He stood at the altar trying not to cry. Their families celebrated. Their pastor prayed over their future. And somewhere between the wedding vows and the final photograph, they believed they were stepping into something wonderful.
They had waited.
No sex before marriage. No crossing the boundaries they believed God had established. No giving themselves sexually to anyone else.
They had heard the warnings about sexual sin. They had listened to sermons about purity. They had been told that waiting would be worth it.
And they genuinely believed it.
But nobody told them what to do when the wedding night didn't feel like a celebration.
Nobody prepared her for the possibility that her body might tense with fear when the man she loved reached for her.
Nobody prepared him for the possibility that the woman who had joyfully promised to spend her life with him might suddenly cry when physical intimacy became real.
Nobody told them that a wedding ceremony could change their covenant status without instantly changing years of learned emotional responses.
And nobody explained why two people who had sincerely tried to honor God could find themselves lying inches apart, feeling more alone than they ever had before.
He wondered, Doesn't she want me?
She wondered, What's wrong with me?
He felt rejected.
She felt defective.
And neither knew how to say what was really happening.
Because how do you admit that the very thing you were taught to save for marriage has become something you dread?
How do you explain that you love your spouse, believe marriage is a gift from God, and still feel frightened when intimacy approaches?
And perhaps the most painful question of all:
If we did everything right, why does this hurt so much?
If that question has ever lived inside your marriage, please keep reading.
Not because one article can repair every wound.
But because Scripture has more to say about your marriage bed than the warnings you heard before your wedding.
And the Jesus who meets sinners with grace is not indifferent to the suffering of husbands and wives who are trying to understand how to love one another.
Somewhere along the way, many sincere Christians learned to talk about sexual purity without learning how to talk about sexual intimacy.
We learned what to avoid.
We learned what not to touch.
We learned where not to go.
We learned that sexual sin matters to God.
And it does.
But some of us were never taught that God also cares about tenderness, mutual delight, patience, dignity, and the emotional safety of the person we marry.
We knew how to say no before the wedding.
We didn't always know how to communicate a loving yes afterward.
And for some couples, that gap became a quiet place of suffering.
Consider the very beginning.
Before sin entered the world, before shame disrupted human relationships, before Adam and Eve hid themselves among the trees, Scripture described something remarkable.
Genesis 2:25 says:
"And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed." (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase is:
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Ve-lo yitboshashu.
"And they were not ashamed."
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say they were naked because they had finally earned the right to be shameless.
It does not say one spouse possessed the other's body.
It does not describe intimacy as a performance to be completed or a demand to be satisfied.
It describes two human beings in a relationship where nakedness was not accompanied by shame.
This is the world before the fall.
Not a world without boundaries, but a world where human vulnerability had not yet become entangled with fear, accusation, and hiding.
Then sin entered.
And one of the first things Scripture records is that Adam and Eve became conscious of their nakedness and attempted to cover themselves.
Later, Adam said to God:
"I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself." (Genesis 3:10, KJV)
Read that again.
"I was afraid."
Fear entered a story that had previously described nakedness without shame.
Genesis does not teach that every sexual difficulty today is the direct result of personal sin. Nor does it establish that all marital intimacy problems come from shame.
But the contrast is deeply revealing.
Human beings were created for relationships marked by trust, yet we now live in a world where vulnerability can become frightening.
And sometimes that fear follows us even into a marriage we entered with genuine love and sincere faith.
For one woman, fear may have grown from years of hearing that sexual desire was dangerous, without being helped to understand that desire within marriage is not inherently sinful.
For another, it may come from childhood experiences, sexual trauma, painful medical conditions, or an overwhelming fear of pregnancy.
For another, it may be the crushing expectation that she must become instantly comfortable with physical intimacy simply because the wedding is over.

For a husband, disappointment may come from unrealistic expectations, performance anxiety, embarrassment, limited sexual knowledge, or the mistaken belief that his wife's hesitation means she does not love him.
And sometimes both spouses are suffering from the same problem.
They are frightened of disappointing each other.
So they stop talking.
She says she's tired.
He turns away.
She feels guilty.
He feels unwanted.
Days become weeks.
Weeks become months.
And eventually the marriage bed becomes a place where both spouses anticipate failure before anything even happens.
The tragedy is not merely that physical intimacy has become difficult.
It is that two people who promised to face life together have begun experiencing their most private struggle separately.
And this is where we must confront a damaging assumption.
Virginity is not the same thing as sexual readiness.
A person can enter marriage without previous sexual intercourse and still lack knowledge about anatomy, arousal, communication, boundaries, pain, emotional vulnerability, or healthy expectations.
Virginity describes an aspect of someone's sexual history.
It does not automatically provide the skills necessary for a mutually satisfying sexual relationship.
And the Bible never promises that couples who abstain before marriage will automatically enjoy effortless physical intimacy afterward.
That promise may have been communicated in certain purity teachings, but it is not a promise Scripture makes.
God's commandments are not vending machines.
We do not insert obedience and receive a guaranteed experience of pleasure on demand.
We obey because God is worthy of obedience.
And when obedience is followed by unexpected suffering, we do not have to pretend the suffering isn't real.
Remember Job.
His suffering could not be explained by the simplistic assumption that faithful people always receive immediate comfort.
Remember the man born blind in John 9.
When the disciples assumed his condition must be connected to someone's sin, Jesus rejected that explanation.
Not every struggle is evidence of disobedience.
Not every disappointment means God is punishing you.
And not every difficult wedding night is a sign that you married the wrong person.
Sometimes you need teaching.
Sometimes you need time.
Sometimes you need healing.
Sometimes you need medical care.
Sometimes you need to unlearn a message that was presented as biblical truth but went further than Scripture itself.
And sometimes you need to hear something that should never have been controversial in a Christian marriage:
Your spouse is a person to be cherished, not a problem to be solved or a body to be claimed.
Listen to the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 7:3–4, he writes:
These verses are sometimes quoted in conversations about marital sexual obligations.
But notice the extraordinary mutuality.
Paul does not place authority only in the husband's hands.
He speaks of husband and wife in corresponding terms.
The Greek of verse 4 includes:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ
Homoiōs de kai ho anēr.
"And likewise also the husband."
That word homoiōs means "likewise" or "in the same way."
Paul's teaching was not an invitation for one spouse to dominate the other.
It placed mutual responsibility at the center of marital intimacy.
And this passage must be read alongside the wider biblical commands to love, honor, and care for one another.
Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
The model is Christ.
Not selfish entitlement.
Not intimidation.
Not impatience.
Christlike love gives itself for the good of the beloved.
That means marital intimacy should never become an excuse for coercion, threats, manipulation, or ignoring a spouse's refusal.
Marriage establishes a covenant of mutual faithfulness. It does not eliminate the need for consent.
A wedding ring is not permission to disregard another person's pain.
And the language of marital duty must never be weaponized against a frightened or suffering spouse.
If your wife is crying because intimacy hurts, the loving response is not to remind her what she owes you.
It is to care about why she is hurting.
If your husband is struggling with anxiety or sexual performance, the loving response is not to ridicule his masculinity.
It is to remind him that his worth is not measured by a sexual performance.
And if either spouse has been pressured, threatened, or forced, that is not merely an intimacy problem. It is a serious violation requiring safety, appropriate support, and accountability.
The Gospel never gives us permission to rename harm as holiness.
Now consider another passage that is often overlooked when Christians talk about sexuality.
Song of Songs 2:16 says:
"My beloved is mine, and I am his." (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ
Dodi li va'ani lo.
"My beloved is mine, and I am his."
There is mutual belonging here.
Affection.
Delight.
The language of lovers who treasure one another.
Throughout the Song, desire is portrayed through poetry, longing, admiration, and celebration.
This is part of the Bible.
The same Scriptures that warn against sexual immorality also preserve a beautiful poetic celebration of love and desire.
Why does that matter?
Because some Christians have absorbed the idea that holiness requires treating all sexual feelings as dirty, even after marriage.
But Scripture makes distinctions.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." (KJV)
The Greek phrase translated "the bed undefiled" is:
ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος
Hē koitē amiantos.
"The marriage bed undefiled."
The word amiantos means undefiled or unstained.
The verse honors marriage while warning against sexual immorality. It does not suggest that faithful marital intimacy is inherently shameful.
Your body did not become evil when you began experiencing desire.
And your wedding ceremony did not suddenly turn something inherently evil into something barely tolerated by God.
Sexual intimacy belongs within God's good design for marriage.
Yet goodness does not mean simplicity.
A gift can be good and still require wisdom to receive and steward.
Marriage itself is good.
But marriage requires learning.
Parenthood can be good.
But parents still need guidance.
Communication is good.
But couples still need to develop the ability to communicate well.
Why, then, would we assume that sexual intimacy is the one area of marriage where two inexperienced people should automatically know everything?
Think about the young bride who lies awake wondering why intercourse hurts.
Perhaps she has been told that pain is simply part of being a woman.
Perhaps she believes she must endure it to be a good Christian wife.
Perhaps she has started to dread bedtime.
She may even feel guilty for praying that her husband will fall asleep before reaching for her.
And because she loves him, she hates herself for feeling relieved when he does.
Someone needs to tell her that persistent or significant sexual pain is not something she is required to endure silently.
Pain with penetration can have multiple causes, including inadequate lubrication, pelvic floor muscle difficulties, vulvodynia, vaginismus, infections, hormonal changes, and other medical conditions.
These are not diagnoses that can be made from an article.
They are reasons to seek compassionate, qualified medical evaluation.
Depending on the cause, treatment may include pelvic floor physical therapy, appropriate medical treatment, education, or psychological support.
There is no spiritual prize for suffering through preventable pain.
And the husband who responds with patience, stops when his wife is hurting, and helps her seek appropriate care is not failing as a husband.
He is practicing love.
Now think about the husband who believed that marriage would finally resolve years of sexual frustration.
He waited because he wanted to honor God.
He expected closeness.
Instead, he encounters hesitation, uncertainty, and repeated disappointment.
At first, he tries to understand.
Then he becomes discouraged.
Then ashamed of his own frustration.
He begins wondering whether his wife finds him unattractive.
He compares their marriage with the cheerful stories other Christian couples tell.
But he does not know that some of those couples have their own struggles behind closed doors.
He does not know how many husbands carry quiet anxiety about erections, ejaculation, desire, or whether they can satisfy their wives.
And he may have never been taught that anxiety itself can interfere with sexual functioning.
So he begins interpreting difficulty as personal failure.
And the more he fears failure, the more difficult intimacy becomes.
What he needs is not another message telling him that real men should always be sexually confident.
He needs truth.
His masculinity is not determined by sexual performance.
His marriage is not a competition.
His wife is not an instrument for proving his worth.
And his identity in Christ is not threatened by the fact that he needs patience, education, or professional help.
This is where grace must become more than a word we sing on Sunday.
Grace must enter the room where disappointment has been living.
Grace must shape the conversation after a difficult night.
Grace must teach a husband how to hear his wife's fear without immediately turning it into an accusation against himself.
Grace must teach a wife how to hear her husband's sadness without automatically interpreting it as a demand.
Grace does not mean pretending that problems are insignificant.
It means refusing to let those problems become the final definition of the relationship.
Imagine what could change if, instead of arguing about whose fault it is, a husband gently said:
"I miss feeling close to you. But I don't want you to be afraid of me. I want us to understand this together."
Imagine if his wife could answer:
"I love you. I'm not trying to reject you. I'm scared, and sometimes I don't even understand why. I need you to be patient with me."
No miracle has instantly occurred.
No medical condition has automatically disappeared.
No deeply rooted fear has vanished.
But something holy has begun.
The truth has entered the conversation.
And honesty is often where healing starts.
James 1:19 instructs believers to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath.
What would happen if we brought that wisdom into our marriages?
If we listened before defending ourselves?
If we asked questions instead of making accusations?
If we stopped measuring marital success by the frequency of intercourse and began paying attention to the quality of our love, honesty, tenderness, and trust?
Sexual intimacy matters in marriage.
It is not something Christians need to dismiss or minimize.
But it is not the whole of marriage.
A marriage covenant is larger than a sexual experience.
A spouse's worth is larger than sexual availability.
And two people can work toward a healthier intimate relationship without treating every difficult evening as a crisis.
For some couples, progress may begin with honest conversations outside the bedroom.
For others, it may mean affectionate touch without the expectation that every moment must lead to intercourse.
For some, it may require the courage to seek help from a qualified healthcare professional or licensed therapist who respects their faith.
For couples facing trauma, the path may involve trauma-informed care and a pace that respects the survivor's safety and agency.
For couples experiencing ongoing conflict, professional marriage counseling may help them recognize patterns of blame, withdrawal, and resentment.
And sometimes the first important step is simply agreeing that neither spouse should be pressured to continue sexual activity when they are frightened, uncomfortable, or in pain.
These are not signs that your marriage is beyond hope.
They are ways of taking your marriage seriously.
But there is another wound we must discuss.
The wound caused when Christians confuse purity with personal superiority.
Some married couples entered marriage as virgins and quietly believed that their sexual history guaranteed a more blessed marriage than those who had previously sinned sexually.
Perhaps nobody said it so directly.
But the implication was there.
We waited. Therefore, our marriage should be better.
And when difficulties appeared, they felt cheated.
But the Gospel was never built on the idea that human beings can earn a trouble-free life through moral achievement.
Sexual abstinence before marriage can be an expression of obedience to God's design.
It is not a purchase price for a perfect wedding night.
And virginity is not a higher form of righteousness that makes someone more worthy of God's love than a repentant person with a sexual past.
The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
We are saved by grace through faith.
Not by sexual history.
Not by marital status.
Not by sexual performance.
Not by our ability to make a marriage look impressive.
By grace.
Through faith.
In Jesus Christ.
That truth humbles the couple who waited.
And it gives hope to the couple who did not.
Because the Gospel is not a story about people who managed to keep themselves perfectly clean.
It is the story of a holy Savior who came to redeem sinners.
Not because every person who struggles with marital intimacy has committed some scandalous sin.
And not because marriage difficulties are evidence of hidden moral failure.
But because Christ enters a world scarred by sin, shame, brokenness, and suffering—and brings redemption to those who trust Him.
Some stories begin with public scandal.
Others begin with private disappointment.
Some wounds come from our own sinful choices.
Others come from what was done to us, from illness, from misunderstanding, or simply from living in a fallen world.
Jesus does not treat every wound as though it has the same cause.
But He calls us to bring our whole lives into His light.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Her relationship history was complicated.
Jesus knew it.
He did not pretend otherwise.
Yet He did not reduce her to that history.
He spoke with her about living water.
He revealed Himself to her.
And the woman who had come to draw water became someone who went back to tell others about Him.
Her story was not finished where her shame might have suggested it was.
Now, John 4 is not a passage specifically about sexual difficulties within Christian marriage.
We should not force it to say what it does not say.
But it reveals something essential about Jesus.
He tells the truth.
He sees the person.
And He offers life.
That is the Savior husbands and wives need.
Not a Savior who tells us to conceal every struggle behind a religious smile.
Not a Savior whose grace depends on our ability to maintain the appearance of a perfect marriage.
But the Savior who calls us out of darkness and into truth.
Perhaps your marriage bed has become a place of disappointment.
Perhaps you have been married for months, even years, and still do not know how to discuss intimacy without tears or arguments.
Perhaps you have wondered whether something is fundamentally wrong with you.
Perhaps you have prayed, "Lord, I tried to honor You. Why is this so hard?"
Hear this carefully.
Your pain is real. But your pain is not your identity.
You are not less of a Christian because your marriage requires help.
You are not less of a woman because intimacy has been frightening or painful.
You are not less of a man because you have experienced sexual difficulty.
And you are not spiritually defective because your wedding night did not resemble the stories you heard.
There is room for both obedience and struggle.
There is room for repentance where sin has occurred.
There is room for forgiveness where genuine wrongs have been acknowledged.
There is room for boundaries where trust has been violated.
There is room for professional treatment where bodies or minds need care.
And there is room for the slow, sometimes uneven work of rebuilding closeness.
Reconciliation does not require someone to remain in an abusive or coercive situation. Forgiveness must never be used to bypass safety, accountability, or justice.
God's grace does not demand that you deny reality.
It invites you to walk in truth.
And perhaps the truth your marriage needs today is surprisingly simple.
You do not have to solve everything tonight.
You do not have to pretend to enjoy something that hurts.
You do not have to prove your love through a performance.
You can begin with a conversation.
A prayer.
An apology.
A medical appointment.
An honest admission that you need help.
You can begin by learning to be gentle with the person you promised to love.
And when you fail to be gentle, you can repent.
When pride has made you harsh, you can confess it.
When resentment has grown, you can bring it into the light.
When fear has silenced you, you can seek the support necessary to speak safely.
Colossians 3:12–13 calls believers to put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, longsuffering, and forgiveness.
Those are not merely virtues for church gatherings.
They belong in the kitchen after an argument.
In the car after a difficult appointment.
In the silence before bedtime.
And yes, in the marriage bed.
A husband who learns patience is not becoming weak.
A wife who learns to communicate her needs is not becoming selfish.
A couple who seeks wise help is not abandoning faith.
They may be learning how to practice it.
And there is something beautiful about two imperfect people who stop demanding that marriage prove their righteousness and start allowing marriage to reveal where they still need Christ.
Because the ultimate purpose of Christian marriage is not to convince the world that Christians never struggle.
It is to honor God through faithful, sacrificial love.
Sometimes that love is joyful and effortless.
Sometimes it requires extraordinary patience.
Sometimes it means celebrating progress that nobody else will ever see.
A night without fear.
A conversation without accusation.
A moment of affection that no longer feels like an obligation.
A husband finally understanding that his wife's pain is not an insult to him.
A wife finally believing that she can speak honestly without being condemned.
Two people praying together after months of emotional distance.
These moments may never appear in wedding photographs.
But they matter.
And they are worth pursuing.
Maybe someone reading this is thinking, I wish we had known these things before we married.
Perhaps.
But you are here now.
And the question is no longer whether you can rewrite your wedding night.
You cannot.
The question is whether you are willing to stop allowing that night—or the painful months that followed—to dictate the rest of your story.
Christ's power to redeem is not limited to the moments before we make mistakes.
His mercy is not exhausted by our ignorance.
His truth is not threatened by our questions.
And His call to love one another remains relevant even when love requires learning things we were never taught.
Romans 12:15 says:
"Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." (KJV)
Some Christian couples need someone to rejoice with them.
Others desperately need someone willing to weep with them.
Not judge them.
Not mock them.
Not rush them.
Not offer simplistic promises that one prayer will fix every physical or psychological difficulty.
Just listen.
Care.
Pray.
And help them find wise support.
If this article has exposed a struggle you have been hiding, you do not need to publish intimate details of your marriage for strangers to read.
But you also do not have to carry your burden alone.
You do not have to explain anything more.
Let those words become a quiet reminder that Christian marriages need grace just as much as every other part of Christian life.
And if you have experienced healing, growth, or restoration, consider sharing a testimony that protects your spouse's privacy.
Someone else may need to know that improvement is possible, even when it takes time.
Perhaps this article brought to mind a married friend who has quietly withdrawn from conversations about relationships.
Perhaps you know a newlywed couple who could benefit from a more compassionate, biblically grounded understanding of intimacy.
Perhaps you know a single Christian preparing for marriage who needs more than warnings about what not to do.
Because discipleship must reach beyond the Sunday sermon.
It must speak to the fears people carry home.
The questions they are afraid to ask.
The struggles they believe no one else understands.
And the grace of Jesus Christ that meets us in the places we are tempted to hide.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build an audience around religious performance, but to keep pointing people toward the truth of Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, healing, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and discipleship accessible to people who need it.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or given you words to share with someone who is struggling, I want to invite you into something deeper.
It is a practical way of helping sustain and expand this ministry so that more people can encounter Scripture-centered encouragement, teaching, and the message of Christ's redeeming grace.
Your giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and free from pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
But out of a shared desire to glorify Christ by making His Word known.
The greatest reason to participate is not the discount.
It is the opportunity to take part in a ministry centered on Jesus Christ.
A single share can place a message of biblical truth and compassion before someone we may never personally meet.
Someone sitting in a quiet bedroom, wondering whether their marriage is hopeless.
Someone afraid to tell their pastor that intimacy hurts.
Someone who has mistaken sexual difficulty for spiritual failure.
Someone who needs to hear that the Lord Jesus Christ does not despise the brokenhearted.
We cannot promise that every share will change a life.
But we can faithfully offer truth and trust God with what happens next.
And now, before you leave, I want to speak to the husband and wife who have made it this far.
Perhaps you are reading separately.
Perhaps your spouse has no idea how much this subject hurts you.
Perhaps you are sitting beside each other, realizing for the first time that you have both been carrying pain.
Do not let this article become another thing you read, agree with, and forget.
If it is safe to do so, turn toward one another.
Ask a question you may have avoided for years.
"What has been hardest for you?"
And then listen.
Do not prepare your defense.
Do not interrupt to explain why you have suffered more.
Do not turn vulnerability into an argument.
Listen.
You may discover that beneath the rejection you felt was fear you never understood.
Beneath the silence was shame.
Beneath the frustration was loneliness.
Beneath the distance was someone who still wanted to be loved but did not know how to ask for help.
And perhaps, by God's grace, you will begin to see your spouse not as the source of all your disappointment, but as another human being in need of compassion, truth, and care.
That does not erase responsibility.
It does not excuse cruelty.
It does not replace medical treatment or professional counseling.
But it can change the way you begin to face the struggle.
Together.
You stood before God and promised to love one another.
You may have imagined that the hardest part of honoring Him would be waiting until marriage.
But perhaps one of the deeper lessons of your marriage will be learning how to love faithfully when the experience is not what you expected.
Learning to be patient when you are disappointed.
Learning to be truthful when you are ashamed.
Learning to ask forgiveness when you have wounded one another.
Learning to receive help without believing you have failed.
Learning that Christian love is not merely a feeling that appears when everything is easy.
It is a commitment shaped by the self-giving love of Jesus Christ.
And above all, learning that your deepest hope is not in the perfection of your marriage.
It is in the perfection of your Savior.
Your marriage cannot save you.
Your virginity cannot save you.
Your sexual fulfillment cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
He died for our sins and rose again, and through Him there is forgiveness and reconciliation with God for all who repent and believe.
That is the foundation beneath every other hope we carry.
So if your marriage has been difficult, do not confuse difficulty with defeat.
Seek the truth.
Pursue wise care.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Extend grace without abandoning healthy boundaries.
And keep bringing your lives before the Lord who is faithful even when the road ahead is uncertain.
You may have entered marriage believing that the wedding night would be the beginning of effortless intimacy.
Instead, you discovered how much there was to learn about vulnerability, patience, and love.
But the story does not have to end in that disappointment.
And perhaps the next chapter will begin not with a perfect romantic moment, but with two people finally telling each other the truth.
Not every wound heals quickly.
Not every marriage is safe.
Not every difficulty has a simple solution.
But no painful beginning has the authority to declare that God is finished working in your life.

You thought the tragedy was that you waited for each other and still found pain. But perhaps the deeper tragedy would be letting that pain convince you that tenderness, truth, and grace are no longer worth pursuing.
